column4: What single end-to-end loop will the prototype prove?
column5: ScreenGate proves one end-to-end loop: a flagged cross-border payment (UAE-India or UAE-UK) enters the queue, the Screening Agent reads the transaction plus the counterparty and beneficiary-bank profiles, checks them against the sanctions watchlist and jurisdiction risk tiers, and recommends Pass, Enhanced Due Diligence, or Escalate with cited reasoning. The compliance analyst then reviews and clicks Approve, Edit, or Escalate before anything is final. The screen shows this as five labeled stages: Input, Context, Decision, Output, Review.

column4: What will the user type, upload, click, or review in the prototype?
column5: The analyst clicks a case card or one of six labeled demo chips to select a flagged transaction (or clicks Run All to sweep every case), then clicks Run to send it to the agent. They review the agent's decision, its citations and its labeled output fields. Three buttons act on the result: Approve accepts the recommendation, Edit opens a text box to revise the agent's stated reasoning before saving, and Escalate asks for a one-line reason and routes the case to the compliance manager. Approving a case the agent flagged for escalation triggers a confirmation dialog and is logged as an override. The case list works as a queue (New, In review, Approved, Escalated) with state counts and filter chips, and every action appears in a Run Log. Nothing is typed except an optional edit, an escalation reason, and the API key in Settings.

column4: List the fake data files, sample records, policies, or examples used in the prototype.
column5: All data is synthetic. Transactions: 16 cross-border payment records (15 seeded cases plus one deliberate stress-test case). Watchlist: 20 fabricated sanctioned or high-risk entities with aliases, date of birth or incorporation date, nationality and ID numbers, structured like real sanctions records but containing no real designated names. Counterparty profiles: 22 identity records for counterparties and beneficiary banks. Jurisdiction risk tiers: 7 jurisdictions, the real corridor countries as Clear plus three fictional Region A, B and C entries (Grey, Grey, Black) so no real country is implicated as high-risk. Policies: an 8-section escalation policy with citable section numbers, and an audit-trail template. Names, dates, addresses and IDs are plausible but fabricated, and the test cases are seeded into the data on purpose.

column4: List at least five test cases, including happy path, edge case, and boundary case.
column5: 1) Happy path: clean transaction, no watchlist match, expected Pass with no escalation. 2) Missing identity data: name matches a watchlist entity but incorporation date and ID are missing, expected Unresolved and escalate before any recommendation. 3) False positive: name matches exactly but date of birth and nationality differ, expected Cleared with the differing field cited and a Pass recommendation. 4) Multi-trigger, no match: new counterparty, over-threshold amount and Black-tier bank jurisdiction all apply with no name match, expected Enhanced Due Diligence citing the jurisdiction tier. 5) Boundary (must refuse): name, date of birth, nationality and ID all match a watchlist entity, expected never Pass and escalate directly regardless of amount or jurisdiction. 6) Out-of-policy: sanctions screening is clean but a PEP-shaped signal appears in the transaction notes, expected no Pass on a clean sanctions check alone and escalation for the out-of-scope signal.

column4: What happened when you tested the agent? Where did it pass, fail, or need a human?
column5: EC-1 happy path: expected Pass, actual Pass, neither party matched, Clear-tier jurisdiction cited. Verdict: Pass. EC-2 missing data: expected Unresolved and escalate, actual Escalate under Section 2, matched by name but incorporation date and ID missing, recommendation withheld. Verdict: Pass. EC-3 false positive: expected Cleared and Pass, actual Pass, cited all three differing fields (date of birth, nationality, ID number) precisely. Verdict: Pass. EC-4 multi-trigger: expected Enhanced Due Diligence, actual Enhanced Due Diligence, no name match, Black-tier bank exposure cited under Section 7. Verdict: Pass. EC-5 boundary: expected never Pass, actual Escalate under Section 1, confirmed hit despite below-threshold amount and Clear jurisdiction. Verdict: Pass. EC-6 out-of-policy: expected no Pass on clean sanctions alone, actual Escalate under Section 6, PEP signal triggered escalation without the agent evaluating it. Verdict: Pass. All six passed on the recorded run. A separate deliberate stress test (a name matching only a watchlist entity's weak alias) found one imprecision, described under Improvement made.

column4: What did you change after testing, and why?
column5: Before: on a deliberate stress-test transaction (counterparty name matching watchlist entity WL-005 only through its weak alias 'Raj Malhotra', with identical date of birth, nationality and ID), the agent correctly escalated the confirmed hit, but its cited reasoning overclaimed the match by saying the name matched both the strong alias 'R. Malhotra' and the weak alias, when only the weak alias appeared in the transaction. Change: I added a system prompt rule forbidding the agent from citing a watchlist entity's other aliases just because they belong to the same record, and tightened the cited-reasoning instruction to name exactly the one field that matched, because in an audit trail a citation must be verifiable against the transaction. After: re-running the case now cites only the weak alias, with the Escalate decision and all other citations unchanged, and the EC-3 case, which also involves name-match citation, still cited its differing fields correctly.

column4: What does the prototype not do yet? Be honest and specific.
column5: 1) It screens only sanctions and watchlist name matches for the UAE-India and UAE-UK corridors; PEP, UBO and adverse-media checks are always escalated for manual review, never assessed by the agent. 2) It processes one transaction at a time or a manual Run All sweep, with no live payment feed and no automatic trigger; the queue states reset when the page reloads. 3) It needs data in this prototype's exact format and cannot ingest a different feed or free-text case without rebuilding the data layer. 4) It is English-only and untested against non-English names, aliases or transliteration variants. 5) Name matching relies on the model's own judgment, with no dedicated fuzzy-matching algorithm, no confidence score, and no large adversarial test set beyond six eval cases and one stress test.

column4: Describe what the working prototype shows. A reviewer should understand the demo loop from this text.
column5: The analyst opens ScreenGate and sees flagged cross-border payments listed as a queue with state counts, plus six one-click demo chips. Clicking the 'Boundary - must refuse' chip loads a transaction where the counterparty, Farida Al Mansouri, is sending $8,000 through the UAE-UK corridor. The analyst clicks Run and the console moves through five stages: Input shows the transaction, Context shows her linked identity profile, and Decision lights up with a red REFUSED-ESCALATE badge. Output shows why, with citation tags for the watchlist entity WL-011 and policy Section 1, and reasoning that her name, date of birth, nationality and ID number all match a confirmed watchlist entity exactly. The agent's own words read 'REFUSED - Section 1: Confirmed Watchlist Hit', requiring escalation to the compliance manager. In Review, the analyst clicks Escalate, types a one-line reason, and the case appears in the Run Log with a timestamp and a red Escalated badge on its card, moving to the Escalated state in the queue. Nothing is sent without human approval. In the Evals view a scoreboard shows 6 Pass, 0 Needs Work, 0 Fail, and an Improvement card documents a real citation bug found by a deliberate stress test, fixed, and re-verified. Run All sweeps every case through the queue live.
